name: Briggs House
location: Northeast corner of Wells and Randolph
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: A five-storey hotel built in 1856. Contemporary fire illustrations show the hotel catching fire; it was rebuilt on the same site.

name: Marine Bank
location: Northeast corner of Lake and LaSalle
fate: Individual fire outcome not yet verified
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The Chicago Historical Society was founded in an office of this bank in 1856. The building rose with Lake Street’s grade in the late 1850s.

name: Col. Wood’s Museum
location: North side of Randolph, east of Clark
fate: Individual fire outcome not yet verified
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: Opened in 1862, the museum combined collections of curiosities with a theatre. Its location is documented by the museum’s pre-fire print.

name: First Methodist Church
location: Southeast corner of Washington and Clark
fate: Individual fire outcome not yet verified
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The congregation used the upper floors as its sanctuary and rented lower floors for shops and offices. A new building followed in 1873.

name: Post Office & Custom House
location: Northwest corner of Dearborn and Monroe
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: Federal offices and courts occupied a building believed to be fireproof. Eyewitness testimony describes fire entering the post office before spreading through the upper floors.

name: Nixon Block
location: Near the northeast corner of Monroe and LaSalle
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: Still under construction during the fire, the Nixon Block largely survived. Its survival makes it an important exception within the downtown burned district.

name: Bryan Block
location: Northwest corner of Monroe and LaSalle
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The first Bryan Block burned within months of opening. The building later erected at this corner was a replacement.

name: Trinity Episcopal Church
location: South side of Jackson, between Wabash and Michigan
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: This church opened in 1860. Following its destruction, the congregation rebuilt farther south.

name: Holy Name Cathedral
location: Northeast corner of State and Superior
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The museum’s before-and-after photographs document the pre-fire cathedral and its ruined shell in the North Division.

name: St. James Episcopal Church
location: Southeast corner of Cass and Huron
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The congregation moved here in 1857. Photographs after the fire show a gutted church with its bell tower standing.

name: Unity Church
location: Southeast corner of Dearborn and Walton
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The church opened in 1867. Robert Collyer preached among the ruins after the fire; surviving masonry was incorporated into its replacement.

name: New England Church
location: Northeast corner of Dearborn and Delaware
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The Congregational church stood just south of Unity Church. The museum’s photograph from the Water Tower shows the ruins of both churches.

name: Grace Methodist Church
location: Northwest corner of Chicago Avenue and LaSalle
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: Dedicated in 1868, the church was destroyed during the fire. The congregation gathered beside its ruins the following Sunday.

name: Isaac N. Arnold House
location: West side of Pine, between Erie and Huron
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: Arnold’s home contained a substantial library, art and Lincoln memorabilia. The Waubansee stone from its garden survived as a fire relic.

name: George F. Rumsey House
location: Huron Street, opposite St. James Church near Cass
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: One of the Rumsey family’s North Division homes. Museum stereographs show the residence before the fire and its ruins afterward; its marker is approximate.

name: McCagg House & Conservatory
location: West side of Clark, between Walton and Delaware
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: The garden conservatory survived much better than the adjoining residence. The two structures must not be assigned the same fire outcome.

name: Terrace Row
location: Michigan Avenue, between Van Buren and Congress
timeNote: The source does not establish a reliable ignition time for this building.
text: This row comprised eleven attached luxury homes, built in 1856. The marker represents the complex, without inventing individual house footprints.
